pages.text: It was debate day in Mr Aryee’s class. The motion was written on the board: “Accra floods because of the people, not the leaders.” Nii Armah and his team stood on the left. Aku and her team stood on the right. Sedinam held the clipboard and kept the time. “Begin,” she said.
sentences: It was debate day in Mr Aryee’s class.
The motion was written on the board: “Accra floods because of the people, not the leaders.” Nii Armah and his team stood on the left.
Aku and her team stood on the right.
Sedinam held the clipboard and kept the time.
“Begin,” she said.
pages.alt: A classroom debate with two teams on opposite sides and a motion written on the board.

pages.text: “It is the people,” said Nii Armah. “Everyone has seen a sachet thrown into a gutter. Everyone has seen someone empty a bucket of rubbish into a drain. Drains carry water only if they are clear. If we keep blocking them, no leader can stop the floods.” His team clapped. “That is true,” said Sedinam quietly, “and we must remember it.”

Everyone has seen someone empty a bucket of rubbish into a drain.
Drains carry water only if they are clear.
If we keep blocking them, no leader can stop the floods.” His team clapped.
“That is true,” said Sedinam quietly, “and we must remember it.”
pages.alt: A pupil points to a picture of a gutter full of plastic while his team nods.

pages.text: “It is the leaders,” said Aku. “Many drains in Accra were built for a smaller city and a lighter rain. An engineer says many of the main drains were designed for a flood that comes about once in twenty-five years, and rain is now heavier. Homes and shops are allowed on waterways and wetlands. Rules exist, but they are not always enforced.” Her team clapped.
sentences: “It is the leaders,” said Aku.
“Many drains in Accra were built for a smaller city and a lighter rain.
An engineer says many of the main drains were designed for a flood that comes about once in twenty-five years, and rain is now heavier.
Homes and shops are allowed on waterways and wetlands.
Rules exist, but they are not always enforced.” Her team clapped.
pages.alt: A pupil points to a drawing of houses built over a stream with a narrow drain running underneath.

pages.text: Mr Aryee raised his hand. “Let us look at the evidence,” he said. “One engineer says silt blocks drains first, and then plastic gets caught in it. A study says over half of the households in flood-prone areas name weak enforcement of land-use rules as the main cause. A news feature says two lagoons have lost over forty per cent of their size to building. And a Ghana Meteorological Agency record shows extreme rainfall events rose by twelve per cent between 2010 and 2025.”
sentences: Mr Aryee raised his hand.
“Let us look at the evidence,” he said.
“One engineer says silt blocks drains first, and then plastic gets caught in it.
A study says over half of the households in flood-prone areas name weak enforcement of land-use rules as the main cause.
A news feature says two lagoons have lost over forty per cent of their size to building.
And a Ghana Meteorological Agency record shows extreme rainfall events rose by twelve per cent between 2010 and 2025.”
pages.alt: A teacher pins four articles to the board, each with a short heading and a number.

pages.text: “So who is right?” asked Nii Armah. “Both of you, and neither of you alone,” said Mr Aryee. “Litter is real, and it makes things worse. Silt is real. Buildings on waterways are real. Drains that are too small are real. And rain is heavier. When people say only one cause is true, they usually protect someone. We need the whole truth.”

“Both of you, and neither of you alone,” said Mr Aryee.
“Litter is real, and it makes things worse.
Silt is real.
Buildings on waterways are real.
Drains that are too small are real.
And rain is heavier.
When people say only one cause is true, they usually protect someone.
We need the whole truth.”
pages.alt: Two pupils shake hands in front of a board that lists several causes joined by arrows.

pages.text: “Then what do we do?” asked Aku. “Citizens must stop blocking drains and must demand that rules be enforced,” said Mr Aryee. “Leaders must keep drains clear, protect wetlands, and build for the rain we have now. Children can write, count, observe, vote one day, and ask questions. A question asked politely and often can move a mountain.”

Children can write, count, observe, vote one day, and ask questions.
A question asked politely and often can move a mountain.”
pages.alt: Children list actions for citizens and leaders in two columns on a chart.

pages.text: Sedinam’s team wrote a letter to the Assembly Member. “Dear Assembly Member,” it began. “We counted twelve blocked drains between our school and the main road. We have stopped throwing rubbish into them. We ask when they will be cleared and whether the big drain near the market will be made wider.” Nii Armah signed it. Aku signed it too.

pages.text: A week later, a reply came. It was short, and it promised a visit. Sedinam grinned. “It is only the first step,” she said. “But now we know that we can speak, and that they can answer.” Mr Aryee smiled. “Debate is good,” he said, “but a letter is better.” The end.
